lead: This unit takes you from one fiber carrying one channel to a fiber carrying many, and then to a whole network of fibers and nodes. By the end you can size a WDM link, choose amplifiers, spot where nonlinearity bites, and read the SONET/SDH and protocol names that appear on every network diagram.
about: Unit 6 turns a point-to-point link into a network. Chapter 6.1 shows how many wavelengths share one fiber and what a multiplexer must do. Chapter 6.2 opens the passive parts that make this possible: couplers, isolators and Bragg gratings. Chapter 6.3 adds optical amplifiers so a wavelength crosses many spans without electronics, and Chapter 6.4 looks at what happens when the power is high enough to bend the glass: self-phase modulation and solitons. Chapter 6.5 sets out the vocabulary of nodes, links and lightpaths. Chapter 6.6 covers SONET/SDH, the synchronous transport that still carries most long-distance traffic, and Chapter 6.7 builds wavelength-routed nodes and switches on top of it. Chapter 6.8 closes with layered protocols and ATM.

chapters.idea: One fiber carries many wavelengths at once, each an independent channel, so capacity grows with the number of channels instead of with electronic speed.
chapters.depth: Definition of WDM and why it exists: the 1550 nm window offers tens of THz, while one laser gives a few Gb/s. Channel spacing and the ITU-T frequency grid around 193.1 THz with 100 GHz and 50 GHz spacing. DWDM versus CWDM (20 nm spacing, 1270-1610 nm, cheap uncoloured optics, short reach). Capacity = N × B, where N is the channel count and B is the bit rate per channel. Multiplexer and demultiplexer principles: prism, diffraction grating, thin-film dielectric filter, arrayed waveguide grating (AWG), fiber Bragg grating. Parameters: insertion loss in dB, adjacent-channel crosstalk in dB, channel uniformity, passband width. Some syllabi say 'wavelength multiplexer' or 'WDM mux/demux' for the same pair.
chapters.figure: blocks, right: N transmitters at λ1…λN into a multiplexer, one single-mode fiber, a demultiplexer, then N receivers; the shared fiber and the multiplexer are picked out.
chapters.example: A DWDM system uses 40 channels on the ITU grid near 1550 nm, spaced 100 GHz apart, each carrying 10 Gb/s. (a) Find the total capacity. (b) Find the spacing in nanometres using Δλ = λ²Δf/c. (c) Find the width of the whole comb. (d) In a 3.2 THz band with 100 GHz spacing, how many 10 Gb/s channels fit? Answers: (a) 40 × 10 = 400 Gb/s. (b) Δλ = (1550×10⁻⁹)² × 100×10⁹ ÷ 3×10⁸ = 0.8 nm. (c) 39 gaps × 0.8 = 31.2 nm, so roughly 1534 nm to 1565 nm. (d) 3.2 THz ÷ 100 GHz = 32 channels, giving 320 Gb/s.
chapters.trap: Converting 100 GHz to a fixed 0.8 nm at every wavelength. The spacing in nanometres grows as λ², so the same grid is wider at 1600 nm than at 1300 nm.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (single-mode fiber, V-number) and Unit 3 (laser sources, external modulators).
chapters.leave: Amplifier gain and noise go to 6.3, coupler and grating physics to 6.2, power budget arithmetic to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Passive parts split, combine, filter and block light without any electrical power, and they decide the loss and crosstalk of a WDM link.
chapters.depth: Fused birefringent and planar couplers: 1×2, 2×2, star and tree shapes. Define coupling ratio, excess loss, insertion loss, directivity and uniformity, each with its dB formula. Isolator: a Faraday rotator between two polarizers, 40-60 dB isolation and 0.5-1 dB insertion loss; why every laser needs one. Circulator: three ports, light travels 1→2→3 only. Fiber Bragg grating: periodic index modulation, Bragg condition λ_B = 2 n_eff Λ, apodization, use as a band-stop filter, as a WDM demultiplexer, and with a circulator as an add-drop multiplexer. Thin-film filters and a one-line mention of tunable Fabry-Perot filters. Only operating principles, no fabrication detail.
chapters.figure: blocks, right: light enters port 1 of a circulator, reaches a Bragg grating that reflects λ2 and passes the rest, port 3 drops λ2, port 2 gives the through channels.
chapters.example: A fused 2×2 coupler receives 1.00 mW at port 1; ports 3 and 4 each give 0.40 mW. (a) Find the coupling ratio. (b) Find the excess loss. (c) Find the insertion loss of one output port. (d) Find the grating pitch that reflects 1550 nm in a fiber with n_eff = 1.45. Answers: (a) 0.40/0.80 = 50:50. (b) excess loss = 10 log₁₀(1.00/0.80) = 0.97 dB. (c) insertion loss = 10 log₁₀(1.00/0.40) = 3.98 dB. (d) Λ = λ_B/(2n_eff) = 1550/(2×1.45) = 534.5 nm.
chapters.trap: Dropping the factor 2 in λ_B = 2 n_eff Λ, and treating excess loss and insertion loss as the same number. One compares total output with input; the other compares a single port with input.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (total internal reflection, single-mode fiber) and Unit 3 (why a laser diode is disturbed by back reflections).
chapters.leave: The system view of a multiplexer is in 6.1, amplifier internals in 6.3, add-drop node design in 6.7.

chapters.idea: An optical amplifier boosts light directly by stimulated emission in a pumped gain medium, so a span does not need a receiver, electronics and a new transmitter.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at this depth. Why amplify: 0.2 dB/km × 80 km = 16 dB per span. Define gain, gain bandwidth, saturation output power, noise figure and polarization dependence. SOA: semiconductor gain chip with anti-reflection coatings, works at 1310 nm and 1550 nm, 20-30 dB gain, noise figure about 6-8 dB, strong polarization dependence, crosstalk between WDM channels, used as booster or in access networks. EDFA: silica fiber doped with Er³⁺, three-level system, pump at 980 nm or 1480 nm, C-band 1530-1565 nm, gain 30-40 dB, noise figure 4-6 dB; parts are pump laser, WDM coupler, doped fiber, isolators, gain-flattening filter; one line on the L-band 1570-1610 nm. Amplifier chains: ASE builds up and OSNR falls as 10 log₁₀ N. State the rule OSNR(dB) = 58 + P_in(dBm) − NF(dB) − 10 log₁₀ N for a 0.1 nm reference at 1550 nm. One line on Raman amplification, pointing to Unit 2.
chapters.figure: blocks, right: 1550 nm signal in, WDM coupler fed by a 980 nm pump laser, erbium-doped fiber, isolator, gain-flattening filter, amplified signal out.
chapters.example: A 10 Gb/s channel enters each EDFA at −20 dBm. Every amplifier gives 20 dB gain with a noise figure of 5 dB, and there are 8 spans. (a) Show that the input power to every amplifier is the same. (b) Estimate the OSNR after the last amplifier in 0.1 nm using OSNR = 58 + P_in − NF − 10 log₁₀ N. Answers: (a) each span loses 20 dB and each amplifier restores 20 dB, so every input is −20 dBm. (b) 10 log₁₀ 8 = 9.0 dB, so OSNR = 58 − 20 − 5 − 9.0 = 24 dB. That clears the roughly 15-16 dB needed for 10 Gb/s at a bit error rate of 10⁻¹², with margin.
chapters.trap: Believing the amplifier regenerates the signal. It restores power, not pulse shape: dispersion and jitter pass straight through, and every stage adds noise, so OSNR drops by 10 log₁₀ N.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 (stimulated emission, laser diode) and Unit 2 (attenuation, dB arithmetic).
chapters.leave: Raman and Brillouin scattering belong to Unit 2, receiver noise and bit error rate to Unit 4, high-power limits to 6.4.

chapters.idea: At high power the fiber refractive index follows the pulse intensity, so the pulse chirps itself; when that chirp cancels group-velocity dispersion, the pulse travels unchanged as a soliton.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Kerr effect: n = n₀ + n₂I with n₂ ≈ 2.6×10⁻²⁰ m²/W for silica. Effective area A_eff and nonlinear coefficient γ = 2π n₂/(λ A_eff), typically 1-3 W⁻¹km⁻¹. Nonlinear length L_NL = 1/(γP₀). Self-phase modulation: nonlinear phase φ_NL = γP₀L_eff, chirp, spectral broadening, and the practical limit it puts on power per WDM channel. Dispersion length L_D = T₀²/|β₂|. Write the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with loss, ∂A/∂z + (α/2)A + (iβ₂/2)∂²A/∂T² = iγ|A|²A, name each term, and do not solve it. Soliton order N² = L_D/L_NL; N = 1 is the fundamental soliton with sech² shape and peak power P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²); soliton period z₀ = (π/2)L_D; N = 2, 3 higher-order solitons breathe. One line each on dispersion-managed solitons and their use in long-haul links.
chapters.figure: plot: pulse width against distance from 0 to 20 km for a 10 ps input; one curve broadens as √(1 + (x/5)²) under dispersion alone, the other stays flat at 1 for the soliton.
chapters.example: A fiber has β₂ = −20 ps²/km, γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹ and pulse parameter T₀ = 10 ps, so the full width at half maximum is 1.763 T₀ = 17.6 ps. (a) Find L_D. (b) Find the peak power of the fundamental soliton. (c) Check that L_NL = L_D. (d) Find the soliton period. Answers: (a) L_D = T₀²/|β₂| = 100/20 = 5 km. (b) P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²) = 20/(2 × 100) = 0.1 W = 100 mW. (c) L_NL = 1/(γP₀) = 1/(2 × 0.1) = 5 km, so N² = 5/5 = 1. (d) z₀ = 1.571 × 5 = 7.85 km.
chapters.trap: Putting average power into γP₀ instead of peak power, and forgetting that a soliton needs anomalous dispersion (β₂ < 0). With normal dispersion the same chirp makes the pulse broaden faster.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (chromatic dispersion, β₂) and 6.3 (amplifiers push power into this regime).
chapters.leave: Brillouin and Raman scattering stay in Unit 2, modulation formats in Unit 3; no numerical solution of the NLS is needed.

chapters.idea: An optical network is a set of nodes joined by fiber links, and each connection is a lightpath that holds one wavelength from end to end.
chapters.depth: Terms every later chapter uses: node, link, span, path, lightpath, channel, wavelength. Topologies: mesh, ring, star, bus, and the difference between physical topology and logical (lightpath) topology. Transparency, opaque networks, regeneration. The public telecommunication network in three tiers: access, metro, core or long-haul, with their typical reach. Node functions: add/drop, cross-connect, regeneration, switching. Protection versus restoration; 1+1, 1:1 and 1:N; why rings dominate metro networks. Broadcast-and-select versus wavelength-routed networks, static versus switched lightpaths. Some syllabi call the lightpath a 'wavelength path' or an 'optical channel'.
chapters.figure: blocks, down: access network with many users, metro ring, core mesh of cross-connects; a lightpath is marked from one access node through to the far side.
chapters.example: A metro ring has 6 nodes. Each node must send one 10 Gb/s lightpath to each of the other five. (a) How many node pairs are there? (b) How many wavelengths are needed if one wavelength per pair carries both directions and there is no wavelength reuse? (c) How many with 1+1 protection? (d) What is the total carried traffic? Answers: (a) 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 pairs. (b) 15 wavelengths. (c) 1+1 sends a copy on a second wavelength, so 30 wavelengths. (d) 15 × 10 = 150 Gb/s of working traffic.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the physical topology with the lightpath topology, and forgetting that protection doubles the wavelength count and the transponder count.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for the wavelength grid; Unit 5 for what a span may lose.
chapters.leave: SONET framing to 6.6, node hardware to 6.7, protocol layers to 6.8.

chapters.idea: SONET/SDH packs many low-rate channels into one frame locked to a master clock, so a single channel can be added or dropped without breaking the whole signal apart.
chapters.depth: Why synchronous: one clock, pointers, byte interleaving. Rates: OC-1 = 51.84 Mb/s, OC-3 = 155.52, OC-12 = 622.08, OC-48 = 2.488 Gb/s, OC-192 = 9.953 Gb/s; STM-1 = 155.52 Mb/s, STM-4, STM-16, STM-64; OC-3 equals STM-1. Frame: 810 bytes as 90 columns × 9 rows, 125 μs, 8000 frames per second; transport overhead 3 columns (section and line), path overhead 1 column, synchronous payload envelope 87 columns = 783 bytes. Pointers and why they allow clock differences; concatenation such as STS-3c. Layers: path, line, section, each monitoring its own bytes. Add-drop multiplexers and rings: UPSR/SNCP and BLSR/MS-SPRing, protection switching within 50 ms. Payload rates: STS-1 SPE 50.112 Mb/s, VC-4 149.76 Mb/s. One line each on jitter and wander.
chapters.figure: stack: photonic WDM at the bottom, then section, line and path above it, each with a short note on what it monitors.
chapters.example: An OC-3 frame is 810 bytes and repeats 8000 times a second. (a) Find the bit rate. (b) Find the payload rate in the 783-byte envelope. (c) What fraction of the frame is overhead? (d) How many 2.048 Mb/s E1 signals does one STM-1 carry if they are packed 3 × 7 × 3? Answers: (a) 810 × 8 × 8000 = 51.84 Mb/s. (b) 783 × 8 × 8000 = 50.112 Mb/s. (c) (810 − 783)/810 = 3.3 percent. (d) 3 × 7 × 3 = 63 E1s, carrying 63 × 2.048 = 129.0 Mb/s; the rest is overhead and stuffing.
chapters.trap: Dividing 155.52 by 2.048 to get the E1 count (that gives about 76 and ignores the multiplexing structure), and placing the pointer bytes inside the payload instead of the overhead.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for the wavelength layer underneath, Unit 3 for line rate versus electronics speed.
chapters.leave: ATM to 6.8, optical cross-connects and wavelength assignment to 6.7.

chapters.idea: A WDM node must add, drop, cross-connect and sometimes convert wavelengths, and the network must give each lightpath one wavelength along its whole route.
chapters.depth: Optical add-drop multiplexer: fixed (one or two wavelengths) and reconfigurable, built with wavelength-selective switches. Optical cross-connect architectures: broadcast-and-select with splitters and gates, and the wavelength-selective switch fabric. Switching elements: MEMS mirrors, liquid-crystal-on-silicon, thermo-optic, electro-optic, semiconductor amplifier gates; compare insertion loss, crosstalk, extinction ratio and switching time. Wavelength continuity constraint, and wavelength converters (optoelectronic regeneration, cross-gain modulation in an SOA, four-wave mixing) that relax it. Routing and wavelength assignment: route first then assign, first-fit, and the graph-colouring view; static versus dynamic traffic. Ring and mesh protection reused from 6.6. One paragraph each on optical burst switching (control packet plus offset time) and optical packet switching.
chapters.figure: graph: nodes A, B, C, D in a line; each edge is labelled with the wavelengths free on that link, and B is drawn as a node with a wavelength converter.
chapters.example: A lightpath must run A-B-C-D. Link A-B has λ1 and λ2 free, B-C has λ2 and λ3 free, C-D has λ1 and λ3 free. (a) Can it be set up with wavelength continuity? (b) What happens if node B has a converter? (c) How many switch elements does a full optical cross-connect need with 4 fiber pairs and 8 wavelengths per pair? Answers: (a) the intersection {λ1, λ2} ∩ {λ2, λ3} ∩ {λ1, λ3} is empty, so it is blocked. (b) use λ1 on A-B, λ2 on B-C, λ3 on C-D; the path works. (c) 4 × 8 = 32 incoming wavelengths switched to 32 outgoing, so 32 × 32 = 1024 elements.
chapters.trap: Declaring a path feasible because each pair of links shares a wavelength. Continuity needs one wavelength common to every link, and only a converter removes that rule.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 (grid), 6.2 (couplers, circulators, gratings), 6.5 (lightpath vocabulary), 6.3 (why conversion may be electrical).
chapters.leave: MEMS and liquid-crystal physics beyond one line, protection schemes already in 6.6, control-plane protocols only named in 6.8.

chapters.idea: Layering gives each network job its own level so one level can change without touching the others, and ATM is the fixed-cell layer-2 standard built to carry voice and data on one optical pipe.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at this depth. OSI seven layers with one line each, and which layer optics touches (physical). Protocol data units: bit, frame, packet, segment. TCP/IP mapping, IP over SONET, IP over WDM, one line on MPLS labels. ATM: the 53-byte cell, a 5-byte header (VPI, VCI, payload type, cell loss priority, header error check) and a 48-byte payload; why cells are short and fixed (voice delay, hardware switching). ATM layers: physical, ATM, adaptation; AAL1 and AAL2 for constant-bit-rate voice, AAL5 for data with its 8-byte trailer. Service classes CBR, VBR-rt, VBR-nrt, ABR, UBR, with a one-line quality-of-service meaning for each. Why ATM lost to IP and Ethernet, and what survived. Two lines on GMPLS and the control plane.
chapters.figure: stack: application, transport, network (IP), data link (ATM cells), physical (SONET over WDM fiber), each with a short note on its data unit.
chapters.example: An IP packet of 1500 bytes travels over AAL5, which adds an 8-byte trailer, with a 48-byte cell payload. (a) How many cells are needed? (b) How many bytes go on the link? (c) What is the efficiency? Answers: (a) (1500 + 8) ÷ 48 = 31.4, so 32 cells after padding. (b) 32 × 53 = 1696 bytes. (c) 1500 ÷ 1696 = 0.884, that is 88.4 percent.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the 5-byte header when counting cell overhead, and forgetting the AAL5 trailer plus padding before dividing by 48.
chapters.prereq: 6.5 (nodes, links, lightpaths) and 6.6 (SONET as the carrier underneath).
chapters.leave: Full TCP/IP behaviour to a data-communication course, switch hardware to 6.7.

links: the multiplexer of 6.1 is built from the couplers and gratings of 6.2
isolators and WDM couplers sit inside every EDFA
amplifier power pushes the fiber into the nonlinear regime
wavelengths become lightpaths once nodes and links are named
SONET supplies the transport layer under those lightpaths
add-drop multiplexers grow into optical nodes and switches
nodes are run by layered protocols, and ATM is one cell layer
soliton limits set the reach a node design must respect
